html:
The westward move of the Banu Hilal, a confederation of Arab Bedouin tribes, from Upper Egypt into North Africa from about 1050. Over the following centuries it spread Arabic speech and nomadic herding across the Maghreb.

The Banu Hilal had come from central Arabia and settled in Upper Egypt. Around 1050 the Zirid rulers of Ifriqiya, roughly today's Tunisia, broke with the Fatimids in Cairo. The Fatimids are said to have let loose the Banu Hilal and their cousins the Banu Sulaym on them. The tribes beat the Zirids in battle in 1052 and sacked Kairouan, home of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, in 1057.

Ibn Khaldun later compared them to a swarm of locusts that ruined farms and towns. Modern historians think he exaggerated, but the tribes did spread over the plains of Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco. They mixed with the Berbers, and over time much of the countryside came to speak Arabic. Their journey is sung in the long Arabic epic of the Banu Hilal, still performed in Egypt and the Maghreb.
